claims.text: A conventional W–Cu composite has directly bonded W and Cu phases.
Direct W–Cu bonding produces relatively high interfacial thermal resistance.
A nanoscale, uniform nickel coating can be introduced at W–Cu interfaces by coating W before consolidation.
Physical vapor deposition or electroless plating are suitable methods for creating the proposed Ni interlayer.
Fusion-reactor joints encounter high temperature, high heat flux, and substantial neutron flux.
A continuous Ni interlayer enhances bonding between tungsten and copper.
The Ni interlayer reduces electron and phonon scattering at the W–Cu interface.
The Ni interlayer improves lattice coupling between tungsten and copper.
Improved lattice coupling from the Ni interlayer lowers W–Cu thermal boundary resistance.
The Ni interlayer acts as a diffusion barrier during processing and irradiation.
The Ni diffusion barrier helps preserve mechanical integrity.
The Ni interlayer delays the formation of irradiation-induced defects.
The Ni-modified composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite without Ni.
The Ni-modified composite will retain mechanical strength comparable to the unmodified W–Cu composite.
The Ni-modified composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to the unmodified W–Cu composite.
The intervention is beneficial when interfacial thermal resistance is the primary limitation on composite thermal conductivity.
A non-uniform or excessively thick Ni coating may compromise the intended improvements.
The optimal Ni thickness, deposition method, and long-term irradiation behavior remain undetermined.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant thermal-conductivity increase greater than 10%, or degradation in mechanical durability or irradiation resistance, would falsify the hypothesis.
